methodological_rigor.justification: The study leverages prospective tumor samples from two multicenter phase III RCTs (CONTINUUM, DIPPER) as discovery and independent validation cohorts, with a further external public cohort (Yeo et al.) for robustness. Consensus clustering was cross-validated using alternative algorithms (k-means, NMF) and a machine-learning classifier was built with separate training/test splits. Statistical analysis is rigorous: Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, Cox models stratified by trial, likelihood-ratio interaction tests, Benjamini-Hochberg multiplicity correction, and multivariable adjustment for T/N category and EBV-DNA. Limitations (endemic population, platform dependence, mechanism unclear) are acknowledged.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a prespecified biomarker analysis embedded in two individual phase III randomized controlled trials (CONTINUUM, DIPPER), supporting LoE 1b for the predictive biomarker claim. The findings (MS1 benefits from anti-PD-1, MS2 spared, MS3 candidate for epigenetic combination) have direct implications for treatment stratification in locoregionally advanced NPC, including a deployed web-based classifier. Predictive interaction (Pinteraction=0.0074 pooled) is clinically meaningful and could inform trial design and practice.

reporting_quality.justification: The authors explicitly state adherence to REMARK guidelines for this biomarker/prognostic study. Patient flow (CONSORT-like Fig 1), BEP representativeness analysis (Table S1), endpoints, covariate adjustment, and interaction tests are transparently reported. Data availability is only partially addressed through a web-based classifier tool; raw RNA-seq data repository accession is not mentioned in the main text, so reproducibility is moderate. Minor gaps include full classifier hyperparameters only referenced in supplement.

novelty_literature.justification: The paper claims the first clinically validated metabolic-subtype classifier predictive of immunotherapy EFS benefit in NPC, built within two phase III trials. It extends prior immune-subtype work (Chen et al., Mol Cancer 2021) by the same group, showing immune subtypes failed to predict long-term benefit while metabolic subtypes did. Biological characterization (amino-acid metabolism in MS1, unsaturated fatty acids in MS2, methylation/one-carbon in MS3) adds mechanistic depth, but the general paradigm of transcriptomic subtyping for ICI prediction is not unprecedented; hence strong rather than field-defining.

writing_presentation.justification: Prose is clear, structured, and follows an IMRaD flow appropriate for a high-impact oncology journal. Abstract, methods, results, figures, and tables are logically organized; statistical results are reported with 95% CIs and HRs. Discussion explicitly links each subtype to actionable clinical strategies and limitations are candidly listed. Figure legends are informative and internally consistent with the text.

key_strengths: Biomarker analysis embedded in two phase III RCTs (CONTINUUM, DIPPER) with independent validation and external dataset replication
Rigorous statistical framework including stratified Cox, likelihood-ratio interaction tests, multiplicity correction, and multivariable adjustment
Clinically actionable stratification: MS1 benefits from anti-PD-1, MS2 spared, MS3 candidate for epi-drug combination
Machine-learning classifier with high accuracy (91-97%) and a deployable web tool for individual-patient prediction
Explicit REMARK reporting and robustness checks across alternative clustering algorithms
key_concerns: Generalizability limited to endemic populations; non-endemic NPC not tested
Raw sequencing data repository and classifier code availability not clearly specified in main text
MS2/MS3 subgroup sizes (17-19%) are modest, limiting precision of non-benefit estimates
Mechanistic link between metabolic state and ICI response remains inferential; functional validation not performed
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically exemplary predictive biomarker study embedded in two phase III RCTs with cross-cohort validation and a deployable classifier; the practice-informing implications and rigor justify tier 1, pending minor reporting/data-sharing clarifications.
